title: Temperature Interval vs Point: Why 1 °C ≠ 1 °F Ever
h1: Temperature interval vs point — the HVAC unit bug that misconfigures PID loops
description: A 1 °C interval always equals 1.8 °F, no 32° offset. Confusing intervals with points is the most common HVAC and process-control unit error.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: 1 °C interval = 1.8 °F interval. But 1 °C point = 33.8 °F. Get them backwards and a 6 °C chiller ΔT becomes a nonsense 42.8 °F swing.
body: Interval and point temperatures look identical on paper but obey different arithmetic. A point is a location on the scale; an interval is a distance between two points. Only the interval survives conversion cleanly by the ratio of degree sizes.

Chiller ΔT specs, thermostat deadbands, PID proportional bands, heat-exchanger approach temperatures, thermocouple accuracy tolerances (±2.2 °C). Every one of these is an interval — plugging a spec sheet's '±2.2 °C' into a UI expecting Fahrenheit points and you have quietly recalibrated the deadband by 30 °F.

A tower designed with a 5 °C approach at 25 °C wet-bulb targets a 30 °C water outlet. Convert the approach as a point (41 °F) and the target becomes 118 °F — nonsense. Convert as an interval (9 °F) and the true 86 °F outlet drops out.
Intervals scale linearly by degree ratio. Points need the offset. When in doubt: ask if the number represents a difference between two temperatures, or a temperature by itself.

faqs.q: Do controllers use interval or point?
faqs.a: Setpoint is a point. Deadband, proportional band, hysteresis, and rate limits are intervals.

faqs.q: Is Rankine an interval or point scale?
faqs.a: Rankine is an absolute point scale like Kelvin. But 1 °R interval = 1 °F interval — the degree size is the same as Fahrenheit.
